paper_title: CoWorld Reasoner: Agentic Multimodal Reasoning with the Evolving Video World Model-Driven Harness

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: As Vision-Language Models (VLMs) advance, they are increasingly expected to perform spatiotemporal reasoning over motion, actions, and view changes beyond what the input images show. Video World Models (VWMs) provide a natural unified engine for visual imagination by generating task-relevant visual content as additional evidence. However, existing approaches typically invoke a VWM through fixed pipelines centered on a predefined form of visual imagination, such as novel-view synthesis. To support flexible visual imagination for diverse reasoning tasks, we introduce CoWorld Reasoner, an agentic framework that uses a VWM as a unified visual reasoning engine. Its Video World Model-Driven Harness exposes multiple visual operations through tools and uses skills to guide the VLM in deciding whether to imagine, selecting an operation, constructing a generation request, and interpreting the resulting visual evidence. We further introduce VLM-VWM Harness Co-Evolution, which jointly revises tools, skills, and execution code based on execution feedback while keeping both model weights fixed. Across seven benchmarks spanning spatial intelligence, temporal and causal reasoning, and perceptual reasoning, CoWorld Reasoner outperforms direct reasoning with the same VLM. The strongest variant improves on all seven benchmarks, including relative accuracy gains of 11.8% on MMSI and 13.0% on ERQA, and outperforms all five evolving baselines using the same backbone across five benchmarks.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong instruction-following and reasoning abilities, but they operate primarily over text. Vision-Language Models (VLMs) extend these capabilities to visual inputs, enabling multimodal understanding and reasoning. Recent VLMs such as Qwen3.8 [1] and Gemini 3.8 [2] can effectively interpret images and analyze charts, and they are increasingly used in real-world multimodal applications. Beyond static image understanding, VLMs are increasingly expected to perform spatiotemporal reasoning over motion, actions, and view changes. For example, model may need to predict whether two objects would overlap if one were moved, reconstruct what happened between two observations, or infer what another viewpoint would reveal. Solving such problems requires going beyond observed visual evidence to reason about unobserved transitions and relations. One promising approach is visual imagination: explicitly generating task-relevant visual predictions Corresponding author. 1 CoWorld Reasoner Figure 1: Illustration of how different multimodal reasoning tasks require different visual operations: (a) view change for spatial perspective taking; (b) interpolation to infer hidden motion between observed endpoints; (c) continuation to predict first contact from observed motion; and (d) intervention to reason about the outcome of controlled change. of what is not observed and using them as additional evidence for reasoning. This raises fundamental question: how can VLM generate and exploit the right visual imagination for the reasoning problem at hand? Video World Models (VWMs), such as MiniMax H3 [3] and LTX-Video [4], provide natural engine for visual imagination by modeling visual dynamics from large-scale video data. Given input images and an appropriate visual operation, they can generate video depicting unobserved views, intermediate states, future events, or intervention outcomes. Recent approaches, including MindJourney [5] and AVIC [6], use VWM to generate additional visual evidence for spatial reasoning, including synthesized views for cross-view reasoning. However, these approaches typically invoke VWM through fixed pipelines centered on predefined form of visual imagination, such as novel-view synthesis. This limits their applicability to diverse reasoning problems, which may require fundamentally different forms of visual imagination: changing viewpoints for perspective taking, interpolating between observations to reconstruct hidden transitions, continuing observed dynamics to anticipate future events, or intervening on the scene to reason about intervention outcomes, as illustrated in Figure 1. visual reasoner should therefore actively determine what 2 CoWorld Reasoner to imagine according to the reasoning problem and how to exploit the generated visual evidence to solve it. To enable task-dependent visual imagination, we introduce CoWorld Reasoner, an agentic framework that uses VWM as unified visual reasoning engine. Unlike an agent confined to fixed workflow, it selects among VWM-driven tools to generate unseen views, intermediate states, continuations, or intervention outcomes according to the question. Skills guide when to invoke these tools, how to construct requests, and how to interpret the generated video; verifier and execution code complete the harness. predefined harness may fail to elicit the visual evidence required by different reasoning tasks or to guide its interpretation. Refinement must coordinate evidence generation and interpretation, because what the VLM can infer depends on what the VWM can reliably generate. We therefore introduce VLM-VWM Harness Co-Evolution, which iteratively refines the interface between the VLM and VWM by jointly revising tools, skills, and execution code based on execution feedback. With both model weights fixed, co-evolution improves how the two models interact and use task-relevant visual evidence. We evaluated CoWorld Reasoner on seven benchmarks spanning spatial intelligence [7, 8, 9, 10], temporal and causal reasoning [11, 12], and perceptual reasoning [13]. Across VLM/VWM variants, CoWorld Reasoner improves aggregate accuracy over direct reasoning with the same VLM. The strongest variant (GPT-5.6 and MiniMax H3) improves all seven benchmarks, with relative gains of 11.8% on MMSI and 13.0% on ERQA. It also outperforms all five evolving baselines using the same backbone on five benchmarks. Further analysis highlights the contributions of generated visual evidence and co-evolved control of its request and interpretation. Our main contributions are summarized below: 1. We leverage VWM as unified visual reasoning engine for visual imagination, enabling the agent to generate task-relevant visual evidence through diverse visual operations. 2. We design Video World Model-Driven Harness that exposes diverse visual operations through standardized tools and encodes reusable reasoning workflows as skills, enabling the agent to decide whether visual imagination is needed, which operation to invoke, and how to interpret the generated visual evidence. 3. We introduce VLM-VWM Harness Co-Evolution, which iteratively refines the interface between the VLM and VWM by jointly revising tools, skills, and execution code based on execution feedback. 4. We evaluate CoWorld Reasoner with multiple VLMs and VWMs across seven benchmarks spanning spatial intelligence, temporal and causal reasoning, and perceptual reasoning, showing gains over direct reasoning and strong performance against evolving baselines, while analyzing the contributions of the harness and its co-evolution.

sections.title:
2.1 Multimodal Reasoning
Recent work uses visual evidence to support multimodal reasoning, particularly spatial tasks.
MVoT [14] and ThinkMorph [15] incorporate generated images into intermediate reasoning steps,
while Omni-R1 [16] uses image generation to unify diverse visual operations. Thinking with Video
[17] uses video generation for visual reasoning. For spatial reasoning, SenseNova-SI [18] and
OpenSpatial [19] use large-scale training datasets, while World2VLM [20] uses views generated
by world models as supervision. At inference time, MindJourney [5] searches camera movements

sections.title:
3.2 VLM-VWM Harness Co-Evolution
VLM-VWM Harness Co-Evolution jointly refines the components that govern visual generation and
evidence use, while keeping the VLM and VWM weights fixed. These components are coupled:
changes to request construction can alter the visual cues available in the generated video, which
in turn affect the guidance needed to interpret and integrate them.
sections.content: Agent execution follows four reasoning stages. At each stage, co-evolution alternates between forward execution and feedback-guided revision. The agent first runs the current harness on the development set. supervisor powered by the same VLM 𝑀 uses the resulting feedback to revise the harness and rerun that stage from the same incoming interaction histories. This cycle can repeat before the supervisor selects the best candidate and passes its harness and histories to the next stage. We repeat these four stages for 𝑅 evolution rounds. Progressive execution. During Capability Boundary Assessment (𝑘 = 1), the agent judges whether the VWM can supply useful missing evidence and may load relevant skill. In Request VWM Assistance (𝑘 = 2), it can revise this assessment before constructing and executing generation request or skipping generation. During Video Interpretation (𝑘 = 3), it reviews the input images and interprets any generated video alongside them, optionally requesting verification. Finally, in Evidence Integration and Reasoning (𝑘 = 4), it combines the input images with generated visual evidence to infer the final answer. sections.title:
4.1 Experimental Setup
Benchmarks. We evaluated CoWorld Reasoner on the seven benchmarks in Table 1. MMSI [7]
assesses reasoning about positions and motion across images; SAT [8] covers ego and object
motion, action outcomes, goals, and perspective taking; and Spin [9] tests perspective taking
under translation and rotation. SpatiaLab [10] uses Multiple-Choice (MCQ) and Open-Ended
(Open) questions about real scenes. ERQA [11] combines spatial, physical, and world knowledge,
while CausalSpatial [12] tests reasoning about collisions, occlusions, and trajectories under object
interventions. PerceptionBench [13] covers counting, attributes, and text reading.
sections.content: Baselines. We compare with five evolving agents adapted to the same GPT-5.6 inputs and scoring protocol (HSI, ReasoningBank, Meta-Harness, ExpeL, and GEPA) and use direct GPT-5.6 reasoning as the reference. The comparison tables also include published results for fine-tuned embodied models, specialist spatial models, and vision-based agents; mechanisms, configurations, and source-protocol notes are provided in Appendix A. Evaluation Protocol. We use 120 development examples, excluded from testing, to evolve CoWorld Reasoner and the five evolving baselines; 30 examples come from each of MMSI, Spin, CausalSpatial, and PerceptionBench. Accuracy is 100 𝑁correct/𝑁; differences are in percentage points, and averages are item-weighted. We measure error recovery as accuracy on the subset of test items that the GPT-5.6 direct reasoning baseline answers incorrectly. sections.title:
4.2 Main Results
Overall Performance. Table 1 shows that CoWorld Reasoner, using its final co-evolved harness,
improves over the GPT-5.6 direct reasoning baseline on all seven benchmarks, especially on MMSI
and ERQA, with gains of 4.54 and 6.75 percentage points, respectively. It leads all five evolving
baselines on five benchmarks and achieves the highest aggregate accuracy. All five evolving
baselines also score below the GPT-5.6 direct reasoning baseline overall. The advantage over
the best evolving baseline reaches 7.07 points on open-ended SpatiaLab. Gains also extend to
SAT, SpatiaLab, and ERQA, which provide no development examples; these results show that the
final harness transfers across benchmarks. Appendix A.6 further compares development and test
performance.
sections.content: Spatial Intelligence. As shown in Table 2, gains span all four MMSI categories and reach 6.56 points for positional relationships. Overall accuracy approaches SenseNova-SIs reported result. SAT perspective taking reaches 84.85%, the highest among the compared methods; goal reasoning also improves, while object motion declines. Accuracy on Spin likewise improves in the View, Mental Rotation, and Perspective categories, as detailed in Appendix A.7. The cross-view skill guides the agent to track object identity and interpret relations in the questions reference frame.

sections.title:
4.3 Analysis
Contribution of VWM-Driven Tools. To assess the contribution of generated visual evidence,
we disabled VWM-driven tools and the verifier while retaining the evolved skills and four-stage
execution. Figure 3a shows the largest tool gains on CausalSpatial Occlusion (Occl.) and Collision
(Coll.). Generated video exposes the intermediate interactions needed to answer these questions.

Gains without tools indicate that harness guidance can also improve reasoning over the input images. VWM-Driven Skill and Tool Use. We measured skill-loading and tool-use rates to examine task-dependent selection. Figure 3b shows that on MMSI, the agent mainly loads cross-view (CV) and temporal (Temp) skills and calls view change (View) and interpolation (Intp) tools to relate views and infer hidden motion. On CausalSpatial, it uses the causal intervention (Caus) skill with intervention (Act) and continuation (Cont) tools to predict intervention outcomes. Skills and tools are rarely used on PerceptionBench, where direct perception often suffices. Effect of VWM Choice. We compared H3 Max Turbo with LTX-2.3 using GPT-5.6, retaining the evolved skills and four-stage execution. Both VWM variants improve overall accuracy and performance on MMSI, Spin, and SpatiaLab, as shown in Figure 3c. The H3 variant yields larger gains across the evaluated benchmarks and also improves SAT, while LTX-2.3 falls below GPT-5. 9 CoWorld Reasoner Figure 3: Analysis of VWM contributions. (a) Subtask gains over Ours (w/o VWM). (b) Skill-loading and tool-use rates by benchmark; tool calls are grouped by visual operation (% of items). (c) Benchmark gains over the GPT-5.6 direct reasoning baseline with two VWMs. on CausalSpatial. These results show that the harness can reuse spatial reasoning workflows across VWMs and benefit from stronger visual generation engine. Recovery from GPT-5.6 Errors. For each benchmark, we evaluated all harness variants and evolving baselines on the subset of test examples that the GPT-5.6 direct reasoning baseline answered incorrectly. CoWorld Reasoner leads on MMSI, SpatiaLab, CausalSpatial, and PerceptionBench (Figure 4). Without VWM tools, it exceeds the evolving baselines on MMSI and SpatiaLab; adding them improves CausalSpatial recovery, leaves SAT unchanged, and reduces ERQA recovery. These CausalSpatial gains mirror the occlusion and collision improvements in Figure 3a: the harness resolves additional GPT-5.6 errors while its overall CausalSpatial accuracy remains close to the GPT-5.6 baseline. Figure 4: Recovery on GPT-5.6 errors; SL combines SpatiaLab MCQ and Open. Harness Transfer Across VLMs. We transferred the GPT-5.6 harness to Grok-4.5 and ran one additional coevolution round before evaluation. Figure 5 shows that item-weighted accuracy rises from 32.86% to 39.78%, with the largest gains on PerceptionBench and Spin. MMSI and CausalSpatial also improve, while SAT declines slightly. The gains span tasks that use the input images directly and tasks that require reasoning about unseen views or outcomes. After adaptation, Grok-4.5 reuses the source harnesss procedures for selecting, interpreting, and integrating visual evidence across benchmarks.

sections.title: 5 Conclusion and Future Work
sections.content: Figure 5: Grok-4.5 accuracy with direct reasoning and the transferred harness. We presented CoWorld Reasoner, which treats VWM as unified visual reasoning engine through Video World Model-Driven Harness of tools, skills, and verifier. VLM-VWM Harness Co10 CoWorld Reasoner Evolution uses execution feedback to improve how the agent requests, evaluates, and integrates visual evidence. CoWorld Reasoner improves over direct reasoning with the same VLM on all seven benchmarks and outperforms all five evolving baselines on five of these benchmarks. Agentic tool use and harness co-evolution extend VWM-based reasoning beyond fixed novel-view synthesis pipelines. Future work will explore test-time training to co-evolve the harness, VLM, and VWM for visual generation and multimodal reasoning across diverse reasoning tasks.

The evolving-agent comparison uses HSI [32], ReasoningBank [33], Meta-Harness [30], ExpeL [34], and GEPA [27], all adapted to GPT-5.6 with the same visual inputs and scoring interface. sections.content: Hierarchically revises task-specific agent harnesses. ReasoningBank Builds and retrieves reusable reasoning memories from agent experience. Meta-Harness Proposes and evaluates changes to executable harness code. ExpeL GEPA Distills insights from task experience and retrieves examples for later tasks. Reflectively revises prompts using execution and evaluation feedback. computed by weighting reported subcategory scores by sample count [18, 7]. MiMo-Embodieds MMSI score and RoboBrain2.0s ERQA score are reported by Li et al. [41]. Avg. is reported for methods evaluated on all benchmarks and weighted by the evaluation sizes in Table 3. A.2 Scoring and Usage Statistics We computed accuracy over all items in each benchmark or category. We normalized multiplechoice answers before comparing them with the correct option. For PerceptionBench, we used deterministic option matching when an answer maps to supplied choice; otherwise, GPT-5.6 judge evaluates correctness under the benchmarks general-QA criterion. The same judge evaluates semantic equivalence for open-ended SpatiaLab questions. The judge operates in an evaluation context fully independent of the task agent. Recovery measures accuracy on the subset of test items answered incorrectly by the GPT-5.6 direct reasoning baseline. When combining SpatiaLab MCQ and Open, we aggregated correct answers and item counts across both formats. Skill-loading rate is the percentage of items on which the corresponding skill is loaded. Tool-use rate is the percentage of items with VWM-driven tool call for the corresponding visual operation. An item can contribute to multiple columns; the Any column counts items with at least one skill load or tool call in the corresponding group. A.3 Agent and Generation Configuration The task agent, co-evolution supervisor, and external answer scorer each use the gpt-5.6-luna deployment in separate contexts. The GPT-5.6 direct reasoning baseline answers each item from the input images in one stage. All five evolving baselines use this GPT-5.6 deployment. Table 5 lists agent and video generation settings. The agent carries its interaction history through stages 14, following the order in Section 3.2. The verifier receives the generated video. The Ours (w/o VWM) variant retains the VWM-driven skills and four-stage execution while disabling all VWM-driven tools and the verifier. We used the MiniMax H3 Max Turbo image-to-video endpoint on FAL. request supplies one source image or two images defining the start and end frames. Generation requests describe the visual transformation without prescribing the task answer. We used 𝑅 = 3 evolution rounds. At each stage, the supervisor evaluates the initial candidate and up to 𝐵 = 5 revisions, with early stopping. For transfer to Grok-4.5, we initialized the harness from the completed GPT-5.6 co-evolution, replaced the VLM with Grok-4.5, and ran one additional co-evolution round before evaluation. 14 CoWorld Reasoner Figure 6: Development and test accuracy. A.5 Stage Assessment and Candidate Selection At each evolution round, the supervisor selects the best completed candidate using stage-specific assessments, sampled traces, and answer-correctness feedback. sections.title: Function
sections.content: VWM-driven skills Cross-view CV Guides reasoning about identity, viewpoint, and layout relations across images. Temporal Temp Guides reasoning about transitions between ordered observations and about short temporal continuations. Causal intervention Caus Guides reasoning about the outcome of specified action on visible target. VWM-driven visual operations View change View Generates new or connecting viewpoint to expose spatial relation. Interpolation Continuation Intervention Intp Generates intermediate states between ordered observations. Cont Extends an observed state forward or backward in time. Act Generates the predicted outcome of specified action on visible target. A.6 Development and Test Performance Figure 6 compares the final evolved agents on the 120 development examples and 8,044 held-out test examples from MMSI, Spin, CausalSpatial, and PerceptionBench. Aggregate accuracy is weighted by the number of examples within each split. ReasoningBank improves over GPT-5.6 on MMSI, Spin, and CausalSpatial during development, yet falls below it on all three test sets. Across the four benchmarks, CoWorld Reasoner and ReasoningBank both reach an aggregate development accuracy of 55.83%, but their test accuracies are 62.88% and 60.95%, respectively, compared with 61.62% for GPT-5.6.
